issues.quote: Then the sky does not feel so hard.
issues.problem: 'Hard' was used one paragraph earlier to mean 'difficult' ('It was very hard to hold'). Here a native writer would say 'heavy'. 'The sky does not feel so hard' reads as if the sky were a hard (solid) object. A beginner will stumble on the double meaning of 'hard'.
issues.fix: Then the sky is not so heavy on me.

notes: A1 comprehension (criterion 7) is acceptable: only a few phrasal items remain. Consider 'took hold of him' -> 'caught him', 'held on' -> 'held him tight', 'At last' -> 'In the end'.
'I want my coat on my shoulders' is the first time the coat is mentioned in A1. One earlier line such as 'Hercules had a big coat.' would make the trick easier to follow.
'A big cup came over the water' can sound as if the cup flew. 'A big gold cup came on the water' or 'came across the water' is clearer.
'another giant, Antaeus': Atlas has only been named, not met. This is acceptable because Atlas was called a giant, but 'a giant, Antaeus' is simpler.

issues.quote: "I want the way to the garden," said Hercules.
issues.problem: A native speaker would not say 'want the way'. It is a calque, and the learner would copy it.
issues.fix: "I want to know the way to the garden," said Hercules.

issues.quote: Then the sky does not feel so hard on them.
issues.problem: A native speaker would say 'heavy' here, not 'hard'. 'Hard' also clashes with the earlier 'Nothing in the world was so hard to hold' (hard = difficult).
issues.fix: Then the sky is not so heavy on them.

notes: Grammar stays within present simple and past simple throughout. 'Each time he touched the ground' is a time clause, not a conditional, so it is fine.
'a coat made from the skin of a lion' and 'a man called Hercules' are reduced participle phrases, not full passives. These are acceptable at B1.
No conditionals or passives were found. The quiz keys are correct and unambiguous.
'wildly' appears twice in two consecutive sentences ('kicking wildly' ... 'beat its wings wildly'). Consider changing the second one to 'beat its wings furiously'.
'The giant said,' directly follows 'the giant stopped a little way off'. Consider 'He said,' instead.
The prose is genuinely literary ('Hardly had Hercules adjusted his hold...', 'bade him a cheerful goodbye') without padding. The transformations (snapping dog, coiling snake) stay gentle.

summary: The retelling follows Hawthorne's version faithfully: the flower-weaving maidens, the shape-shifting Old Man of the Sea, Antaeus, the golden cup, Atlas, and the coat-cushion trick. It is age-appropriate at all levels. A1 and A2 fail only on small natural-English points: 'the sky does not feel so hard' should use 'heavy', and A2's 'I want the way to the garden' needs fixing. B1, B2 and C1 pass.
